column1: # Where each note in lex-ang.tsv was checked.
# A note is the sentence printed under a woven Old English word: in the
# tooltip, on /old-english/<word> — joined to the descent sentence, or under
# "Worth knowing" where the word has no descendant — in the note column of the
# descent hub, and, when it says "meant", "simply" or "literally", as the
# word's line in the discoveries feed. It is a published claim, and until
# 2026-10-25 nothing recorded that any of the Old English ones had been looked
# up against a dictionary, where the Latin ones have named theirs in
# On 2026-10-25 all 87 were read, the 39 of the verbs, adjectives, adverbs,
# numerals and interjections first and the 48 of the nouns after: against
# the entry each row's gloss was read in
# (ang-glosses.tsv), against etymonline for every English word a note
# explains, against English Wiktionary's English entries where etymonline
# does not print the claim — "the quick and the dead", "to wit", the
# proverb — and against Bosworth–Toller where the gloss was read there.
# etymonline was read in the Internet Archive's copies of its pages
# (web.archive.org, snapshots of 2025-08 to 2026-03), because that day the
# site answered every automated reader with a challenge page; the entries
# are cited as etymonline's all the same, being its text. 84 stood. Three did
# not, and are listed at the foot of this file with what the dictionaries
# say, so that nobody restores one in good faith.
# The line repeats the note. That is the point: reword a note and it has no
# source until somebody opens the dictionary again and says which entry.
# Each line names the entries it was checked against, separated by spaces:
# tests/tools/ang-notes.test.ts requires every note of a held part of speech
# to have a line repeating it, a line to cite an entry its row's gloss was
# read in — a Wiktionary page holds every word of one spelling, and hund is a
# dog where hund² is a hundred — and a note that names its row's etymon to
# cite that English word's own entry, etymonline's or Wiktionary's. What a
# note is held to is what the entries say: one they contradict, hedge or say
# less than is rewritten, and a loose paraphrase of a true thing stands, as
# "“bleak” is its Norse cousin" does for an English word borrowed from the

column4: “mann” meant a human being of either sex
literally “woman-person”
from “frēon”, to love
“wīf” meant woman generally, and was neuter
the householder, not yet the spouse
originally simply “woman, wife”
“hlāf-weard”, the loaf-keeper
the near-dweller
“fēond” was any enemy before it meant a demon
the healer; the bloodsucking worm may be a different word
it survives in “lychgate”, the corpse-gate of a churchyard
the usual word; “docga” was rare and gave “dog”
borrowed straight from Latin; “lion” came later, from French
“a nadder” was misheard as “an adder”
also meant serpent and dragon
“mete” meant food of any kind
“brēad” meant a morsel
any fruit, not only the apple
it became Middle English “ey”, which Norse “egg” displaced
survives in many English place-names in -ham
literally “eye-hole”; “window”, “wind-eye”, is Norse
a seat, bench or throne; “settle” for the high-backed bench dates from the 1550s
usually traced to “beech”
the moon was masculine, the sun feminine
“sky” came later, from Old Norse
the Kentish Weald keeps the word
its dative, “byriġ”, survives in many place-names as -bury
an enclosure, whence the -ton of place-names
literally “age of man”; “wer”, man, survives in “werewolf”
a realm; it survives as the -ric of “bishopric”
common in English place-names
“shade” comes partly from it
from one new moon to the next
“tīd” was an hour or a season, whence Yuletide
it gave “morn” and “morrow”, and “morning” was built on “morn”
whence “evening” and “eve”
years were counted in winters
the peace of a place, as in Frithstool
“forsooth” and “soothsayer” keep it
borrowed from Old Norse
“feoh” was cattle, then property, then money; “fee” is partly this word
“asking”, built on “ask”, replaced it
its second half comes from “swerian”, to swear
it meant a story; “gōd spell”, the good story, became “gospel”
“drēam” meant joy and music; nobody has proved it became “dream”
it shares a root with Latin “somnus”, sleep, whence “somnolent”
“ire” is not this word: it came from French
“gift” came from its Norse cousin
“many a little makes a mickle”
“grēat” meant thick or massive
“weak” came from its Norse cousin, “veikr”
the suffix in “hopeless” is this word
it meant powerful before it meant wealthy
“sad” is another word, “sæd”, which meant sated, full
it shares a root with “hāl”, whole
“cwic” meant alive, as in “the quick and the dead”
also “hale”; and “hǣlan”, to make whole, became “heal”
“blāc”, with a long vowel, meant pale; “bleak” is its Norse cousin
“to wit”, “unwittingly”
“numb” was its past participle, taken or seized; “take” itself is Norse
it meant to count, as in “bank teller”
“wyrċan” gave both “work” and “wrought”
it meant to roll or toss
it meant to advise, as in “Ethelred the Unready”
it meant to scratch or incise
“steorfan” simply meant to die
“sellan” meant to give
“ġieldan” meant to pay or repay, and became “yield”
“close” is partly this word and partly Old French “clos”
related to “tācn”, a token or sign
“winnan” meant to struggle or toil
“warden” and “guard” are its cousins, through French
it meant to look at, not to display
as “besēċan” it became “beseech”
“wend one’s way”; its past tense “went” was captured by “go”
“weorpan” meant to throw
its past participle gave “fang”, once a seizing or taking
“ne ǣfre”, not ever
“sōna” meant immediately
“nēah”, near, became “nigh”
“all āna” became “alone”
the usual word for the number; English kept “hundred”, “a counting of 100”
“former” began as its comparative
literally “be whole”; “wassail” is its Norse cousin, “ves heill”
said at parting as well as meeting: “wesaþ hāle”, to more than one, glosses Latin “valete”, farewell

#                    descent hub and the launch draft call mete and cwic false friends, so
#                    the feed told both as plain descents. mete's says what it said in the

#                    sustenance", the narrower flesh sense "attested from c. 1300". The fact
#                    about cwic sat on swift, woven for "quick", where the feed read it as
#                    "swift became English swift, but “cwic” meant alive"; it is cwic's now,
#                    etym:quick: Old English cwic "living, alive, animate", the speed sense
